noi_dung:
Investigating Chan Requires Returning the Light Inward

Walking, standing, lying, sitting,

Never apart from it;

Apart from it—

At once a mistake.

What is "it"? It is the hua-tou we use to apply effort in Chan investigation. Cultivate the Way with the true mind: raise up the hua-tou and investigate unbrokenly, unceasingly. Hour after hour, minute after minute, second after second—not a stray thought, not a discursive thought intruding; in short, in thought after thought, only the single hua-tou as the topic of investigation. Then where is there time to chat with one another and disturb others? No chance either to laze and rest, still less to gossip about rights and wrongs—single-heartedly holding the hua-tou to awaken. There is a verse:

All matters pass smoothly by;

Hard to cast off is temper.

If truly never angered—

That is a precious jewel.

Harboring no hatred,

All matters flow.

Afflictions never arise—

Whence grievances?

Ever blaming others,

Suffering without end.

Only with such an attitude can the Chan investigator hope one day to "enter the gate." In the Chan Hall, everyone must return the light and reflect it inward—turning back upon themselves, asking: am I applying effort, or letting my mind run after discursive thoughts? Look at yourselves: am I shining the light to illumine myself—not shining outward? This demands our utmost heed.

Applying effort in the Chan Hall, remember these two lines:

Mahasattvas pay others no mind;

With Amitabha, each looks to himself!

Moment after moment, manage yourselves—no need to mind anyone else, still less to trouble others, for that obstructs everyone's effort and may cost them their chance at enlightenment—unacceptable. As I often tell you:

Sincerely admit your own faults;

Never discuss the faults of others.

Others' faults are my own faults;

Same substance is called Great Compassion.

If everyone held this thought, all would cultivate single-heartedly, thinking of nothing else—no more busy gossip disturbing others.

The Chan investigator must squarely face one fundamental issue. What issue? That is habitual tendencies. Sitting in Chan removes habitual tendencies and bad habits, purifies the mind, and undoes the ugly habit of envying those better than ourselves. Cast off envious minds, afflicted and ignorant minds—all of them. Only then will the True Mind show, wisdom appear, and the meditator have hope of good news.

Why do people love gossip about rights and wrongs? Precisely from delusion. Why does jealousy arise? Also from delusion. Why the wish to harm others? Delusion, all of it. Whatever is unreasonable springs from delusion. Then whence delusion? Precisely from refusing to practice samadhi, and so lacking wisdom—and so we circle forever in self and others, right and wrong, never getting out. Therefore we must return the light inward, facing our past faults, resolving to reform, instead of stubbornly clutching ugly habits and refusing to let go.

Why do you doze when sitting in Chan? Because in seeking the Dharma your hearts are not true. If you sincerely sought the Way, you would never doze. Try it and see—am I right or not?

Chan Session talks, December 1980
